In this holy month of Ramadan, Muslims gather around a table, waiting impatiently for the moment to break the fast. Chez Sharifa*, l’excitation est à son co: At Sharifa’s*, excitement is at its peak. She has prepared a table laden with succulent dishes to welcome her loved ones and friends. It’s a typical iftar**, with a queer touch.
C’est dans la trentaine que Sharifa, mèr: Sharifa, a mother of three, revealed her sexual orientation in her thirties. Often faced with questions about her sexuality, she admits that for a long time she didn’t know how to define herself outside of heteronormativity. “To be honest, when I was young, I was quite homophobic. I even remember writing an essay against homosexuality at CEGEP. That was in the 1990s, so there were no academic repercussions,” she confides.
Plus jeune, elle avait demandé une fois: When she was younger, she once asked her father how he would react if he had a gay child. His answer, although reassuring on the surface, tore Sharifa apart. “My father simply answered that he would keep providing for them, but I understood that it meant he wouldn’t accept it.” Sharifa adds: “Looking back, I realize that asking that question was already a sign of my attraction to people of the same sex, but I didn’t know how to accept and live this identity in harmony with my other identities.”
Elle explique que son homophobie reposai: She explains that her homophobia was based on a mix of ignorance and cultural rejection. As a member of a visible minority, both racially and religiously, she experiences exclusion from the dominant culture. Her very existence left her feeling countercultural, marginal, which pushed her to reject her homosexuality and the concept of queerness in general, which she strongly associated with the West. Sharifa admits she internalized all sorts of propaganda and expresses her shame as she acknowledges: “I didn’t think you could be Muslim, Indian and queer. I couldn’t imagine it. I couldn’t imagine myself.”
<strong>« Être <em>queer</em> a été une: “Being queer has been a blessing for my Islam”
C’est en rentrant à l’université que Sha: It was when she started university that Sharifa began to diversify her circle of friends and gradually open up to LGBTIQ2S communities. She adds that she had “so many gay friends” that she often found herself defending them, notably against her sister, who considered their existence haram, that is, religiously forbidden.
« J’ai alors commencé à enquêter sur le: “So I started looking into the subject to convince her otherwise. And one day, during my research, I came across an interpretation that really touched me. That’s when I realized that I was queer myself. By making sense of all this from an Islamic perspective, I was finally able to claim this identity and avoid a large part of the guilt and shame that sometimes come with it,” she explains in a relieved tone.
Tout au long de son mariage (avec un hom: Throughout her marriage (to a man), and even after the birth of her three boys, the suspicions of those around her about her sexual orientation persisted. Her ex-husband himself questioned her about her sexuality, but she always forcefully denied that part of herself. “I thought everyone had attractions to people of the same sex and that it didn’t necessarily mean a queer identity,” explains the woman in her forties.
« Le fait d’être <em>queer</em> a été un: “Being queer has been a blessing for my Islam. It made me a stronger Muslim. I got to know my faith better because I questioned it and I questioned the homophobia that was supposedly inherent to it. That’s when I learned that Islam and homosexuality were not antitheses. I grew closer to Allah, I deepened my religion and my faith,” she says in a jubilant voice.
À la suite de son divorce, et avant même: After her divorce, and even before she considered herself queer, rumours about her sexual orientation spread because of her non-straight circle. “A friend at the time came to talk to me about it and told me how disgusting it was to spread such horrible rumours,” she confides.
Elle explique qu’elle avait plus de faci: She explains that it was easier for her to openly defend the queer cause when it wasn’t about her. “I felt like I was defending someone else; I didn’t realize how harmful those words were,” she admits.
Elle souligne toutefois que, pour de nom: She points out, however, that for many people in her community, trauma has almost become a culture in itself. “In the context of Islam in the West, Muslims tend to conform to the image of ‘the Other’ that the West has assigned to them,” explains the Muslim woman. “Obviously, that doesn’t excuse this behaviour and it gives a bad connotation to a peaceful religion.”
Cette situation affecte grandement sa re: This situation greatly affects her relationship with the Muslim community. “While I was living with my partner and we were a couple, I hid it from my longtime friend. Eventually, I told her, but I was hesitant and a little scared. Her reaction surprised me. She just laughed and reassured me,” says Sharifa. The experience made her aware of her own behaviour and the resulting internalized Islamophobia, since she wouldn’t have had such doubts with white or non-Muslim friends. “By hesitating, I denied her the right to be gay herself, to support LGBTIQ2S+ people and to be open-minded. It only reinforces the mistaken image of Islam in the Western collective imagination, making the religion look intolerant,” she says sadly.
Bien qu’elle travaille sur l’islamophobi: Although she is working on the Islamophobia she has internalized, Sharifa unfortunately cannot control how others perceive her. As an Indian woman, especially when she wears the hijab, she faces rejection from some members of the LGBTIQ2S+ community. “Time and again, people in the queer community have told me I had to choose, that I couldn’t be both Muslim and queer, or that I wasn’t queer enough. Once, at a queer event, a white, non-Muslim person came up to me to ask why I was there, and started denying my queer identity on the grounds that I am obviously Muslim and don’t sufficiently conform to Western norms of queerness.”
D’ailleurs, c’est cette façon de voir le: In fact, it is this way of seeing things that allows her to keep going to traditional mosques. “I think some people at my neighbourhood mosque know I’m queer, but no one has paid any attention. Especially since I’ve brought my ex-girlfriend with me several times,” she explains. For Sharifa, queer Muslim spaces are nonetheless her favourite places. “Before, there was no queer Muslim space. There are more and more virtual spaces that I go to,” she says. “Now, there are a few in-person events. I’ve met a lot of friends at iftars, Eids and other queer Muslim celebrations. I love these spaces so much, where I don’t have to choose between my identities; I feel like myself, I feel at home!” Sharifa exclaims cheerfully, smiling softly.
« J’aimerais qu’il y ait des espaces con: “I wish there were spaces dedicated to queer Muslims, and even a mosque that would welcome everyone. Everyone deserves the right to feel whole and safe, with no compromise.”
La nuit se déploie doucement, tandis que: Night gently unfolds as the last prayer of the day begins. Sharifa and her children follow the lead of her friend, who guides them in prayer, reciting one surah after another. She reaffirms her faith in the face of Western Islamophobia and of homophobia within the Muslim community itself, one prayer at a time.
<strong>Un homosexuel de couleur et musu: A gay, Muslim man of colour CAN know happiness
Nofel, un jeune Arabo-Canadien d’origine: Nofel, a young Arab Canadian of Libyan origin, proudly embraces his identity as an openly gay Muslim man. His happiness, however, is often criticized. “It happens frequently that when I reveal my identity as a gay Muslim, people don’t understand how a man of colour can be gay and feel joy. They ask me why I so openly express my satisfaction at being Muslim, as if I were boasting about a trait that everyone frowns upon,” he explains.
Le poète souligne que cette incompréhens: The poet points out that this lack of understanding shows up in all queer spaces, including queer Muslim spaces. “In the experience of homosexuality, suffering is often elevated to an identity, to a culture in its own right. People don’t recognize that a gay Muslim man of colour can know happiness. It’s discouraging to see that the collective imagination has yet to take in the possibility of joy among Muslims who also identify as racialized queer people,” he says sadly.
Nofel n’a jamais eu à faire de compromis: Nofel has never had to compromise between his sexuality and his religion. “I grew up in Libya, and religion was always present. The subject of sex was never discussed, at least not around me, whether it was heterosexuality or homosexuality. So I never learned that homosexuality was a sin,” says the 25-year-old. He recounts that when he realized he was gay, he was so happy that he announced it to everyone around him. “I don’t like to say that my family accepted my homosexuality. For me, there is nothing to accept: I am who I am, that’s it. There is no room for negotiation,” he says with a smile and a confident air.
<strong>La mosquée est un lieu où l’amou: The mosque is a place where love exists
Le jeune homme évoque un raisonnement ré: The young man brings up a line of reasoning common in queer Muslim communities: “Even if we’re rejected at the mosque, we’ll create our own spaces.” This raises the question, however, of who exactly is rejecting them at the mosque. “In my experience, I haven’t faced that rejection. Obviously, that doesn’t mean it doesn’t exist.” In his view, many gay Muslims distance themselves from their religious identity because of rumours and negative stereotypes. “This self-exclusion needs to be deconstructed,” he says.
Il partage son expérience romantique dan: He shares his romantic experience in Muslim places of worship. “At a queer iftar, I met a man on the prayer mat. We only dated for a few weeks, and all our dates took place in mosques. We were welcomed with open arms every time. You could say we weren’t an openly gay couple, but rather two close friends at the mosque, especially since, in Arab culture, men can be affectionate with one another without being seen as romantically involved. That, obviously, in no way rules out the possibility of love at the mosque. The very fact that we were there shows that the mosque is a place where love exists and will continue to exist,” says the Muslim man.
Momin Rahman, professeur de sociologie à: Momin Rahman, a sociology professor at Trent University, has been studying the experiences of gay Muslims in Canada for 16 years. As a gay man who is culturally Muslim and of Bengali origin, he became interested in the subject from a perspective of representation.
« Il est important de comprendre que l’e: “It’s important to understand that the experience of queer Muslims is complex and diverse. Rather than seeing this community as a minority within a minority, we need to think of it intersectionally,” he says right away.
Rahman, tout comme Sharifa, a également: Rahman, like Sharifa, also noted that for many members of Muslim communities, homosexuality is seen as a Western identity and way of life, which creates additional tensions. He explains that “this is the result of a lack of information. In reality, many Muslim cultures have a history of gender and sexual diversity, but it is little known because of Western propaganda, which lays claim to queerness.”
De plus, la racisation nuit à l’acceptat: What’s more, racialization hinders the acceptance of queer Muslims by Westerners, which complicates the situation. “Not having the support of their ethno-religious community affects queer Muslims’ mental well-being,” he says.
Selon le sociologue, plusieurs participa: According to the sociologist, several participants in his study say they experience deep alienation. “Many have lost the space they need to express the Islamophobia and xenophobia they face. They feel abandoned and isolated. Some people suffer great pain during communal festivities and religious ceremonies such as Ramadan and Eid.”
Malgré ces difficultés et alors que cert: Despite these difficulties, and even as some abandon religion because it becomes too heavy a burden, many LGBTIQ2S+ Muslims insist on reconciling their Muslim and queer identities by interpreting Islamic texts in ways that fit their understanding.
« Nous inclure avec notre identité à par: “Including us with our full identity avoids a whole range of social problems. As queer Muslims, we hold a lot of power,” he says, stepping out of his role as educator with a big smile.
Sharifa souhaite ardemment qu’un autre e: Sharifa ardently hopes that another space like the Unity Mosque/el-Tawhid Juma Circle will emerge in Montréal. Since its founding in Toronto in 2009, this mosque has championed gender equality, recognizes LGBTIQ2S+ people and gives voice and leadership to marginalized people, while ensuring their safety by keeping the mosque’s location confidential. Imam El-Farouk Khaki, co-founder of the mosque, explains that the project was born of a personal need: “A big part of my activism is about finding spaces where I can be myself, without having to hide my political convictions, my sexual orientation, my values and my spirituality.”
Au départ, El-Farouk Khaki n’était pas i: Initially, El-Farouk Khaki was not an imam, but after the founding of the Unity Mosque, several members of the community asked that he be designated as one. “The queer and trans Muslim community had needs that weren’t being taken into account,” explains the gay man, who is also the founder of Salaam, the first gay Muslim group in Canada. He cites in particular religious marriage (nikah) for same-sex couples, which requires the presence of an imam and legal recognition to be made official. He insists that at his mosque, “equality prevails, there is no hierarchy, no power dynamic, anyone can deliver a sermon and lead a prayer.” Then he adds: “The title of imam is just a formality; it doesn’t necessarily come with authority.”
Par ailleurs, son travail d’avocat spéci: In addition, his work as a lawyer specializing in refugee defence has shed light on how people are dehumanized and how religion is used as a weapon against different kinds of people, not just because of their sexual orientation. “I have witnessed the trauma, distress and suicidal thoughts that stem from the weaponization of religion.” His activism, combined with his faith, gave him the motivation he needed to found a safe and inclusive space for everyone, whether within his religious community or elsewhere.
Alors que le mois béni du ramadan touche: As the blessed month of Ramadan draws to a close, the imam extends a helping hand and offers comforting, inspiring words to those who, in the face of adversity, continue to persevere in their religious practice.
« L’islam est un voyage, pas une destina: “Islam is a journey, not a destination to be reached in haste. The Quran was revealed to the Prophet over a period of 23 years, so let patience be your guide. Not everything needs to make sense right away. In Islam, there is no original sin. Instead, we are born in forgetfulness. Remember to be gentle with yourself. We have the unique ability to choose our perception of God and to understand it better. As we deepen our faith, we discover that Allah frequently presents Himself as ‘Rahman’ and ‘Rahim,’ two of the preferred conceptualizations of the Creator. These Arabic words, which come from the expression ‘mother’s womb,’ imply the same deep sense of compassion and care that a mother may feel for her child. Community is vital on this path, because we are not alone in this quest. Whether in person or online, find people who support and encourage you. Salam and Eid Mubarak,” concludes Imam El-Farouk Khaki.
Dans le ciel paisible de la nuit, une no: In the peaceful night sky, a new moon graces us with its presence, signalling the arrival of Eid al-Fitr.
